claim: Strong induction of apoptosis in the posterior compartment of the Drosophila wing disc causes apoptosis of cells in the anterior compartment.
source: Strong induction of apoptosis in one compartment of the Drosophila wing disc causes apoptosis of cells in the other compartment, indicating that dying cells can release long-range death factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript and shown in figures.

claim: Dying cells can release long-range death factors.
source: Strong induction of apoptosis in one compartment of the Drosophila wing disc causes apoptosis of cells in the other compartment, indicating that dying cells can release long-range death factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that apoptosis in one compartment induces apoptosis in a distant compartment.

claim: Eiger is the Drosophila tumor necrosis factor (TNF) homolog.
source: We identified Eiger, the Drosophila tumor necrosis factor (TNF) homolog, as the signal responsible for apoptosis-induced apoptosis (AiA).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Eiger's identity.

claim: Eiger is the signal responsible for apoptosis-induced apoptosis (AiA).
source: We identified Eiger, the Drosophila tumor necrosis factor (TNF) homolog, as the signal responsible for apoptosis-induced apoptosis (AiA).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Eiger is required for AiA.

claim: Eiger is produced in apoptotic cells.
source: Eiger is produced in apoptotic cells and, through activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, is able to propagate the initial apoptotic stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing Eiger expression in apoptotic cells.

claim: Eiger activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway to propagate the initial apoptotic stimulus.
source: Eiger is produced in apoptotic cells and, through activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, is able to propagate the initial apoptotic stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing JNK pathway activation and its requirement for AiA.

claim: During coordinated cell death of hair follicle cells in mice, TNF-α is expressed in apoptotic cells.
source: We also show that during coordinated cell death of hair follicle cells in mice, TNF-α is expressed in apoptotic cells and is required for normal cell death.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing TNF-α expression in apoptotic hair follicle cells.

claim: TNF-α is required for normal cell death during coordinated cell death of hair follicle cells in mice.
source: We also show that during coordinated cell death of hair follicle cells in mice, TNF-α is expressed in apoptotic cells and is required for normal cell death.
evidence: This is supported by TNF-α neutralization experiments showing impaired hair follicle cycle progression and decreased apoptosis.

claim: AiA provides a mechanism to explain cohort behavior of dying cells seen in normal development and under pathological conditions.
source: AiA provides a mechanism to explain cohort behavior of dying cells that is seen both in normal development and under pathological conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Apoptosis is a distinct form of programmed cell death in which cells activate an intrinsic suicide program to self-destruct.
source: Apoptosis is a distinct form of programmed cell death in which cells activate an intrinsic suicide program to self-destruct.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about apoptosis.

claim: Apoptosis plays a major role in development and tissue homeostasis.
source: This process plays a major role in development and tissue homeostasis, and abnormal regulation of apoptosis is associated with a variety of human diseases (Fuchs and Steller, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Abnormal regulation of apoptosis is associated with a variety of human diseases.
source: This process plays a major role in development and tissue homeostasis, and abnormal regulation of apoptosis is associated with a variety of human diseases (Fuchs and Steller, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Dying cells can secrete signals that stimulate the recruitment of phagocytes (find-me signals).
source: Dying cells can secrete signals that will stimulate the recruitment of phagocytes (find-me signals) as well as expose signals on their surface to facilitate their engulfment (eat-me signals) (Lauber et al., 2003; Ravichandran, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Dying cells can expose signals on their surface to facilitate their engulfment (eat-me signals).
source: Dying cells can secrete signals that will stimulate the recruitment of phagocytes (find-me signals) as well as expose signals on their surface to facilitate their engulfment (eat-me signals) (Lauber et al., 2003; Ravichandran, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Apoptosis has been traditionally regarded as a silent process that does not affect surrounding tissues.
source: However, apoptosis has been traditionally regarded as a silent process that does not affect surrounding tissues.
evidence: This describes historical scientific perspective.

claim: Apoptotic cells are the source of signals that can have profound effects on their neighbors.
source: Only more recently has it become clear that apoptotic cells are the source of signals that can have profound effects on their neighbors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work and the current study.

claim: Cells that undergo apoptosis in response to stress and injury can secrete mitogenic and morphogenetic signaling proteins to stimulate growth and tissue repair.
source: Cells that undergo apoptosis in response to stress and injury can secrete mitogenic and morphogenetic signaling proteins to stimulate growth and tissue repair (Bergmann and Steller, 2010; Morata et al., 2011; Greco, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Apoptotic cells secrete Wnt, Dpp/Bmps and Hedgehog (Hh) proteins as mitogenic factors.
source: These factors include Wnt, Dpp/Bmps and Hedgehog (Hh) proteins, which all play major roles in the regulation of growth and patterning during development (Huh et al., 2004; Perez-Garijo et al., 2004; Ryoo et al., 2004; Fan and Bergmann, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wnt, Dpp/Bmps and Hedgehog (Hh) proteins play major roles in the regulation of growth and patterning during development.
source: These factors include Wnt, Dpp/Bmps and Hedgehog (Hh) proteins, which all play major roles in the regulation of growth and patterning during development (Huh et al., 2004; Perez-Garijo et al., 2004; Ryoo et al., 2004; Fan and Bergmann, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mitogenic signaling by apoptotic cells has been reported for a diversity of animals, from Hydra, to flat worms, Drosophila and vertebrates.
source: Mitogenic signaling by apoptotic cells has been reported for a diversity of animals, from Hydra, to flat worms, Drosophila and vertebrates, and it has been implicated in regeneration, wound healing and tumor growth (Tseng et al., 2007; Chera et al., 2009; Bergmann and Steller, 2010; Li et al., 2010; Pellettieri et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mitogenic signaling by apoptotic cells has been implicated in regeneration, wound healing and tumor growth.
source: Mitogenic signaling by apoptotic cells has been reported for a diversity of animals, from Hydra, to flat worms, Drosophila and vertebrates, and it has been implicated in regeneration, wound healing and tumor growth (Tseng et al., 2007; Chera et al., 2009; Bergmann and Steller, 2010; Li et al., 2010; Pellettieri et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Large groups of cells often undergo coordinated death during development and under conditions of severe tissue injury.
source: On the other hand, large groups of cells often undergo coordinated death during development and under conditions of severe tissue injury (Glucksmann, 1951; Jacobson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The elimination of the tadpole tail during amphibian metamorphosis is an example of group suicide behavior in normal development.
source: Classic examples for such group suicide behavior in normal development include the elimination of the tadpod tail during amphibian metamorphosis, and the removal of interdigital membranes during digit individualization in vertebrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about developmental biology.

claim: The removal of interdigital membranes during digit individualization in vertebrates is an example of group suicide behavior in normal development.
source: Classic examples for such group suicide behavior in normal development include the elimination of the tadpod tail during amphibian metamorphosis, and the removal of interdigital membranes during digit individualization in vertebrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about developmental biology.

claim: In Drosophila, apoptosis plays a crucial role in several morphogenetic events, sculpting tissues and organs.
source: In Drosophila, apoptosis plays a crucial role in several morphogenetic events, sculpting tissues and organs, removing a large number of cells in a coordinated manner and inducing cellular reorganization (Lohmann et al., 2002; Link et al., 2007; Manjon et al., 2007; Suzanne et al., 2010; Suzanne and Steller, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The regressive phase of the hair follicle (HF) is an example of communal death in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, another example of communal death is the regressive phase of the hair follicle (HF), which undergoes cycles of growth (anagen), degeneration (catagen) and rest (telogen) (Hardy, 1992; Fuchs, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The hair follicle undergoes cycles of growth (anagen), degeneration (catagen) and rest (telogen).
source: In vertebrates, another example of communal death is the regressive phase of the hair follicle (HF), which undergoes cycles of growth (anagen), degeneration (catagen) and rest (telogen) (Hardy, 1992; Fuchs, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In catagen, all the cells in the lower portion of the HF are eliminated by apoptosis.
source: In catagen, all the cells in the lower portion of the HF are eliminated by apoptosis (Lindner et al., 1997; Botchkareva et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In coordinated cell death, cell death takes place in a very rapid and highly synchronized manner.
source: In all these cases, cell death takes place in a very rapid and highly synchronized manner.
evidence: This is an observation about the nature of coordinated cell death.

claim: It is not known how cohort behavior of dying cells is achieved.
source: However, it is not known how this cohort behavior is achieved.
evidence: This describes a gap in scientific knowledge.

claim: Many pathological states are associated with extensive cell death, which leads to severe damage and can have grave consequences for patients.
source: Likewise, many pathological states are associated with extensive cell death, which leads to severe damage and can have grave consequences for patients.
evidence: This is general medical knowledge.

claim: Examples of pathological states associated with extensive cell death include alcohol-/drug-induced liver failure, viral infection, cardiac infarction, ischemic stroke and cachexia.
source: Examples include alcohol-/drug-induced liver failure, viral infection, cardiac infarction, ischemic stroke and cachexia (Sharma and Anker, 2002; Kang and Izumo, 2003; Guicciardi and Gores, 2005; Yuan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In pathological states with extensive cell death, apoptosis accounts for widespread cell loss and is thought to contribute to patient mortality.
source: In all these pathologies, apoptosis accounts for widespread cell loss and is thought to contribute to patient mortality (Thompson, 1995; Favaloro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Undead cells are apoptotic cells that are kept alive by the expression of the baculovirus caspase inhibitor p35.
source: To reveal novel types of signaling induced by apoptotic cells we made use of 'undead' cells: apoptotic cells that are kept alive by the expression of the baculovirus caspase inhibitor p35 (Hay et al., 1994).
evidence: This is the experimental definition used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: In undead cells, cells initiate the apoptotic cascade but cannot execute cell death because the activity of effector caspases is blocked.
source: Under these conditions, cells initiate the apoptotic cascade but cannot execute cell death because the activity of effector caspases is blocked.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of undead cells.

claim: Apoptotic cells are normally very rapidly cleared in living tissues.
source: Although apoptotic cells are normally very rapidly cleared in living tissues, undead cells persist for long times and thereby permit analysis of signaling events associated with the induction of apoptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about apoptosis.

claim: Undead cells persist for long times and thereby permit analysis of signaling events associated with the induction of apoptosis.
source: Although apoptotic cells are normally very rapidly cleared in living tissues, undead cells persist for long times and thereby permit analysis of signaling events associated with the induction of apoptosis.
evidence: This is the rationale for using undead cells in the study.

claim: Expression of hid and p35 in the posterior compartment of wing imaginal discs results in ectopic Wg expression.
source: As expected, we observed ectopic Wg expression and discs with abnormal and in many cases overgrown posterior compartments due to increased cell proliferation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of hid and p35 in the posterior compartment of wing imaginal discs results in discs with abnormal and in many cases overgrown posterior compartments due to increased cell proliferation.
source: As expected, we observed ectopic Wg expression and discs with abnormal and in many cases overgrown posterior compartments due to increased cell proliferation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Undead cells contain high levels of cleaved caspases.
source: Undead cells contain high levels of cleaved caspases and were visualized by staining with activated caspase-3 antibody, which recognizes cleaved effector caspases as well as the activity of the initiator caspase Dronc (Figure 1B) (Fan and Bergmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation.

claim: Activated caspase-3 antibody recognizes cleaved effector caspases as well as the activity of the initiator caspase Dronc.
source: Undead cells contain high levels of cleaved caspases and were visualized by staining with activated caspase-3 antibody, which recognizes cleaved effector caspases as well as the activity of the initiator caspase Dronc (Figure 1B) (Fan and Bergmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Large numbers of apoptotic cells are observed in the anterior compartment when undead cells are generated in the posterior compartment.
source: Surprisingly, we also observed large numbers of apoptotic cells in the anterior compartment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Two large clusters of dying cells are typically seen in the wing pouch when undead cells are generated in the posterior compartment.
source: Under these conditions, we typically saw two large clusters of dying cells in the wing pouch.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Cells in the wing pouch region are more susceptible to apoptosis, as indicated by higher rates of cell death after X-irradiation and hid over-expression.
source: It appears that cells in this region of the wing disc are more susceptible to apoptosis, as indicated by the fact that higher rates of cell death within this region were also observed after X-irradiation and hid over-expression (Milan et al., 1997; Moon et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Active caspase-3 immunoreactivity is cytoplasmatic and diffuse in undead cells.
source: Although active caspase-3 immunoreactivity was cytoplasmatic and diffuse in undead cells, the staining of cells in the anterior compartment was punctate and intense, indicating that these cells are dying (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The staining of cells in the anterior compartment with active caspase-3 is punctate and intense, indicating that these cells are dying.
source: Although active caspase-3 immunoreactivity was cytoplasmatic and diffuse in undead cells, the staining of cells in the anterior compartment was punctate and intense, indicating that these cells are dying (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and inference from staining pattern.

claim: Undead cells in the posterior compartment do not show TUNEL staining.
source: As expected, undead cells in the posterior compartment did not show TUNEL staining, but caspase-3-positive cells in the anterior compartment also displayed distinct TUNEL labeling (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Caspase-3-positive cells in the anterior compartment display distinct TUNEL labeling.
source: As expected, undead cells in the posterior compartment did not show TUNEL staining, but caspase-3-positive cells in the anterior compartment also displayed distinct TUNEL labeling (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Undead cells in the posterior compartment of the Drosophila wing disc have the ability to stimulate the induction of apoptosis at a distance in a different compartment.
source: These findings indicate that undead cells in the posterior compartment of the Drosophila wing disc have the ability to stimulate the induction of apoptosis at a distance in a different compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Expression of rpr along with p35 using the hh-Gal4 driver produces extensive cell death in the anterior compartment.
source: Expression of the pro-apoptotic gene rpr along with p35 using the same driver also produced extensive cell death in the anterior compartment (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Non-autonomous apoptosis is not restricted to the wing imaginal disc.
source: Furthermore, non-autonomous apoptosis is not restricted to the wing imaginal disc, as we also observed apoptosis in the anterior compartment of other discs, such as the haltere or the leg discs (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Apoptosis is observed in the anterior compartment of haltere and leg discs when undead cells are generated in the posterior compartment.
source: Furthermore, non-autonomous apoptosis is not restricted to the wing imaginal disc, as we also observed apoptosis in the anterior compartment of other discs, such as the haltere or the leg discs (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Apoptosis is not observed in the eye-antennal discs when undead cells are generated in the posterior compartment.
source: On the other hand, we did not observe apoptosis in the eye-antennal discs, suggesting this is not a general systemic response (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Non-autonomous apoptosis is not a general systemic response.
source: On the other hand, we did not observe apoptosis in the eye-antennal discs, suggesting this is not a general systemic response (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eye-antennal discs do not show non-autonomous apoptosis.

claim: Non-autonomous apoptosis is not compartment specific.
source: However, this phenomenon is not compartment specific.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments using different compartments.

claim: Expression of hid and p35 in the dorsal compartment using ap-Gal4 driver produces widespread apoptosis in the ventral compartment.
source: We used the apterous-Gal4 (ap-Gal) driver to express hid and p35 in the dorsal compartment of wing discs. In this case, we observed widespread apoptosis in the ventral compartment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The use of weaker drivers (such as Ci-Gal4 and en-Gal4) produces very little non-autonomous apoptosis.
source: However, the use of weaker drivers (such as Ci-Gal4 and en-Gal4) produced very little non-autonomous apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: A strong apoptotic stimulus is required to induce non-autonomous apoptosis.
source: This suggests that a strong apoptotic stimulus is required to induce non-autonomous apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that weaker drivers produce little non-autonomous apoptosis.

claim: Cells that die in the anterior compartment express the anterior marker Ci-Gal4, demonstrating that they are of anterior origin.
source: Importantly, we observed that cells that die in the anterior compartment express the anterior marker Ci-Gal4, demonstrating that they are of anterior origin, and not 'escaping undead cells' (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The apoptosis taking place in the anterior compartment is indeed non-autonomous apoptosis.
source: This confirms that the apoptosis taking place in the anterior compartment is indeed non-autonomous apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dying cells are of anterior origin.

claim: Milan et al. (1997) reported non-autonomous apoptosis upon ricin overexpression, which they explained as being an indirect consequence of changes in proliferation during compartment size accommodation.
source: Milan et al. (1997) reported non-autonomous apoptosis upon ricin overexpression, which they explained as being an indirect consequence of changes in proliferation during compartment size accommodation.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: Downregulation of dMyc leads to a reduction of cell and tissue size.
source: dMyc is a key regulator of tissue growth, and downregulation of dMyc leads to a reduction of cell and tissue size (Johnston et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of hid and p35 together with dMyc RNAi in the posterior compartment results in a significantly reduced compartment size but still shows large numbers of apoptotic cells in the anterior compartment.
source: Therefore, we generated posterior compartments that express hid and p35 together with dMyc RNAi. Under these conditions, we still observed undead cells, as revealed by cleaved caspase-3 staining, in a compartment with significantly reduced size (Figure 4A). Importantly, despite the size reduction, we still saw large numbers of apoptotic cells in the anterior compartment (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Size compensation does not cause non-autonomous cell death in this system.
source: These observations argue strongly against the idea that size compensation causes non-autonomous cell death in this system.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that non-autonomous apoptosis occurs even when compartment size is reduced.

claim: Downregulation of Wg or Dpp in the posterior compartment does not rescue non-autonomous apoptosis.
source: To examine this notion, we made experiments downregulating Wg or Dpp signals in the posterior compartment (Figure 4B,C). Under these conditions we failed to rescue non-autonomous apoptosis, which demonstrates that it is not a consequence of morphogenetic apoptosis or depends on the levels of Wg or Dpp (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Non-autonomous apoptosis is not a consequence of morphogenetic apoptosis or depends on the levels of Wg or Dpp.
source: To examine this notion, we made experiments downregulating Wg or Dpp signals in the posterior compartment (Figure 4B,C). Under these conditions we failed to rescue non-autonomous apoptosis, which demonstrates that it is not a consequence of morphogenetic apoptosis or depends on the levels of Wg or Dpp (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that downregulating Wg or Dpp does not rescue non-autonomous apoptosis.

claim: Generation of undead cells in the posterior compartment for a shorter period of time (3–4 days) results in discs that have a normal pattern, size and proliferation rates in the posterior compartment but still show induction of ectopic apoptosis in the anterior compartment.
source: We also generated undead cells in the posterior compartment for a shorter period of time (3–4 days) to address the possibility that changes in growth, development and patterning could result in non-autonomous apoptosis. For this purpose, we employed the Gal4/Gal80TS system to temporally control transgene expression (McGuire et al., 2003). Under these conditions we were able to generate discs that have a normal pattern, size and proliferation rates in the posterior compartment. Nevertheless, we again observed the induction of ectopic apoptosis in the anterior compartment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and citation.

claim: Apoptosis-induced non-autonomous apoptosis is not the consequence of cell competition, abnormal development, morphogenetic apoptosis or size compensation to prune excessive growth.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that apoptosis-induced non-autonomous apoptosis is not the consequence of cell competition, abnormal development, morphogenetic apoptosis or size compensation to prune excessive growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the various control experiments performed.

claim: Genuine apoptotic cells have the capacity to induce non-autonomous apoptosis at a distance.
source: Hence, we conclude that genuine apoptotic cells have the capacity to induce non-autonomous apoptosis at a distance.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments using rpr or hid alone without p35.

claim: Expression of rpr or hid alone for 48–72 hr generates large numbers of apoptotic cells in the posterior compartment and induces apoptosis in the anterior compartment.
source: For this purpose, we induced apoptosis in the posterior compartment by expressing rpr or hid alone, without p35. To allow for larval viability, we again used the conditional Gal4/Gal80TS system to express pro-apoptotic proteins for only 48–72 hr. Under these conditions, large numbers of apoptotic cells were generated in the posterior compartment, and again we saw the induction of apoptosis in the anterior compartment (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The amount of non-autonomous apoptosis with genuine apoptotic cells is generally less prominent compared to the use of undead cells.
source: In this situation, the amount of non-autonomous apoptosis was generally less prominent compared to the use of undead cells, but in some cases it reached very high levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The JNK pathway is activated during stress-induced apoptosis in Drosophila.
source: To gain insight into the underlying molecular mechanism, we considered a role of the JNK pathway since it is activated during stress-induced apoptosis in Drosophila and plays a role for the induction of Dpp and Wg in apoptotic cells (Ryoo et al., 2004; Perez-Garijo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The JNK pathway plays a role for the induction of Dpp and Wg in apoptotic cells.
source: To gain insight into the underlying molecular mechanism, we considered a role of the JNK pathway since it is activated during stress-induced apoptosis in Drosophila and plays a role for the induction of Dpp and Wg in apoptotic cells (Ryoo et al., 2004; Perez-Garijo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: puckered (puc) is the sole Drosophila JNK-specific MAPK phosphatase.
source: puckered (puc), the sole Drosophila JNK-specific MAPK phosphatase, is a feedback antagonist of the JNK pathway (Martin-Blanco et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: puckered is a feedback antagonist of the JNK pathway.
source: puckered (puc), the sole Drosophila JNK-specific MAPK phosphatase, is a feedback antagonist of the JNK pathway (Martin-Blanco et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The puc-lacZ line serves both as a mutant for puckered and as a read-out for JNK activity.
source: Hence, the puc-lacZ line, which is an insertion in the puckered gene (pucE69), serves both as a mutant for puckered and as a read-out for JNK activity.
evidence: This is the rationale for using puc-lacZ in the study.

claim: Very high puc-lacZ staining is observed in undead cells, where the apoptotic loop keeps JNK constantly activated.
source: As expected, we saw very high puc-lacZ staining in undead cells, where the apoptotic loop keeps JNK constantly activated (Shlevkov and Morata, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and citation.

claim: Modest activation of JNK is observed in dying cells in the anterior compartment.
source: However, we also observed modest activation of JNK in dying cells in the anterior compartment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A trail of puc-lacZ activity is sometimes observed between undead cells and dying cells.
source: Sometimes we also saw a trail of puc-lacZ activity between undead cells and dying cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In a puc+/− background, the amount of apoptosis in the anterior compartment is dramatically increased compared to wild-type.
source: Normally, the generation of undead cells in the posterior compartment for 72 hr causes only a modest induction of apoptosis in the anterior compartment (Figure 6B). However, in a puc+/− background, the amount of apoptosis in the anterior compartment was dramatically increased (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: JNK is involved in the induction of non-autonomous apoptosis.
source: This suggests that JNK is involved in the induction of non-autonomous apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that increasing JNK activity increases non-autonomous apoptosis.

claim: Apoptosis in the anterior compartment is completely blocked in male larvae hemizygous for hep1.
source: Strikingly, apoptosis in the anterior compartment was completely blocked in male larvae hemizygous for hep1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: hep1 hemizygous mutants retain diffuse staining with caspase-3 in the posterior compartment, demonstrating that the generation of undead cells is not suppressed.
source: Importantly, hep1 hemizygous mutants retained diffuse staining with caspase-3 in the posterior compartment, demonstrating that the generation of undead cells is not suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation.

claim: The JNK pathway plays an important role in AiA.
source: Collectively, these experiments indicate that the JNK pathway plays an important role in AiA.
evidence: This is inferred from the various JNK manipulation experiments.

claim: Blocking JNK activity specifically in the anterior compartment completely abrogates non-autonomous apoptosis.
source: To block JNK activity in the anterior compartment, we drove expression of the RNAi of basket (bsk), the Drosophila JNK. Under these conditions, non-autonomous apoptosis is completely abrogated (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: JNK is required for cells to die in the anterior compartment as a consequence of AiA.
source: Since here we are not affecting JNK activity in undead cells, we can conclude that JNK is required for cells to die in the anterior compartment as a consequence of AiA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking JNK in the anterior compartment prevents non-autonomous apoptosis.

claim: One way by which the JNK pathway is activated in Drosophila is through the TNF ligand Eiger.
source: One way by which the JNK pathway is activated in Drosophila is through the TNF ligand Eiger.
evidence: This is established knowledge about JNK pathway activation.

claim: Over-expression of Eiger can induce cell death through activation of the JNK pathway.
source: Significantly, over-expression of Eiger can induce cell death through activation of the JNK pathway (Igaki et al., 2002; Moreno et al., 2002; Kauppila et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In vivo roles for Eiger-induced cell death have been elusive.
source: However, in vivo roles for Eiger-induced cell death have been elusive (Igaki et al., 2009; Maezawa et al., 2009; Keller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Significant up-regulation of Eiger is observed in undead cells.
source: Indeed, we saw significant up-regulation of Eiger in undead cells, consistent with the idea that Eiger may be produced by dying cells as a signal to induce non-autonomous apoptosis (Figure 7A′′).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The elimination of eiger function completely abrogates the non-autonomous apoptosis in the anterior compartment.
source: To critically test this hypothesis, we generated undead cells in the posterior compartment of wing discs homozygous mutant for eiger. Strikingly, the elimination of eiger function completely abrogated the non-autonomous apoptosis in the anterior compartment (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: Loss of Eiger does not impair JNK activation and mitogen production within undead cells.
source: Importantly, under these conditions we still observed overgrown posterior compartments and a large amount of ectopic Wg signaling, as well as diffuse caspase staining, in undead cells (Figure 7E). This indicates that loss of Eiger does not impair JNK activation and mitogen production within undead cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that undead cells still show Wg signaling and caspase staining in eiger mutants.

claim: AiA is significantly decreased by inhibiting Eiger specifically in undead cells.
source: Consistent with our model, we observed that AiA was significantly decreased by inhibiting Eiger specifically in undead cells (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Eiger is a key signal that is generated by apoptotic cells to induce apoptosis of other cells at a distance.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that Eiger is a key signal that is generated by apoptotic cells to induce apoptosis of other cells at a distance (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is inferred from the various Eiger manipulation experiments.

claim: The mouse hair follicle (HF) is an ideal system for investigating AiA since cohort cell death naturally occurs at precise times in the HF cycle.
source: The mouse hair follicle (HF) is an ideal system for investigating AiA since cohort cell death naturally occurs at precise times in the HF cycle (Lindner et al., 1997; Botchkareva et al., 2006; Tong and Coulombe, 2006).
evidence: This is the rationale for using the HF system, supported by citations.

claim: During catagen, apoptosis leads to degeneration of the lower two-thirds of the HF while the upper part remains intact.
source: During catagen, apoptosis leads to degeneration of the lower two-thirds of the HF while the upper part remains intact (Lindner et al., 1997; Tong and Coulombe, 2006) (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The upper part of the HF that remains intact during catagen encompasses the bulge, which houses the HF stem cells required for the generation of the new HF.
source: This portion encompasses the bulge, which houses the HF stem cells required for the generation of the new HF (Rompolas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The first catagen phase commences at postnatal day 16 (P16).
source: The first catagen phase commences at postnatal day 16 (P16) and hence we isolated skin at this time point.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HF development.

claim: At P16, HFs with a large number of apoptotic cells can be easily detected.
source: At P16, we could easily detect HFs with a large number of apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Apoptotic cells in the HF at P16 display apoptotic morphology such as membrane blebbing, condensed nuclei and are positive for cleaved caspase-3.
source: These cells displayed apoptotic morphology such as membrane blebbing, condensed nuclei and were positive for cleaved capase-3 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The HF cycle is dependent upon TNF signaling.
source: It was previously shown that the HF cycle is dependent upon TNF signaling (Hoffmann et al., 1996; Ruckert et al., 2000; Tong and Coulombe, 2006), but the cellular source of TNF-α has not been determined.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The cellular source of TNF-α in the HF cycle has not been determined prior to this study.
source: It was previously shown that the HF cycle is dependent upon TNF signaling (Hoffmann et al., 1996; Ruckert et al., 2000; Tong and Coulombe, 2006), but the cellular source of TNF-α has not been determined.
evidence: This describes a gap in scientific knowledge.

claim: Apoptotic cells in the HF express high levels of TNF-α.
source: We examined TNF-α expression and found that apoptotic cells in the HF expressed high levels of TNF-α (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: TNF-α is not detected at any other location besides apoptotic cells in the HF.
source: Significantly, TNF-α was not detected at any other location besides apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Apoptotic cells are the source of pro-death signals during catagen.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that apoptotic cells are the source of pro-death signals during catagen and that AiA contributes to the destruction of the HF.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TNF-α is expressed in apoptotic cells.

claim: AiA contributes to the destruction of the HF during catagen.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that apoptotic cells are the source of pro-death signals during catagen and that AiA contributes to the destruction of the HF.
evidence: This is inferred from the TNF-α expression and neutralization experiments.

claim: Neutralizing TNF-α in vivo impairs the HF cycle progression as a result of decreased apoptosis.
source: Neutralizing TNF-α in vivo impairs the HF cycle progression as a result of decreased apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C-F.

claim: At P17.5, control dorsal skin HFs display a morphology typical for late catagen.
source: Antibodies were injected daily from P14-P17 and, as expected, at P17.5 control dorsal skin HFs displayed a morphology typical for late catagen (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Upon inhibition of TNF-α, HFs escape destruction and have a morphology reminiscent of anagen or very early catagen.
source: In contrast, upon inhibition of TNF-α HFs escaped destruction and had a morphology reminiscent of anagen or very early catagen (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Inhibition of TNF-α results in a clear loss of synchronicity in tail HFs.
source: We next extended this analysis to tail HFs. We analyzed tailskin whole mounts and observed again an inhibition in the destruction of the HF and also a clear loss of synchronicity (Figure 9E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E-G.

claim: TNF-α inhibited animals have dramatically reduced numbers of cleaved caspase-3-positive cells compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, TNF-α inhibited animals had dramatically reduced numbers of cleaved caspase-3-positive cells, indicating that TNF-α promotes apoptosis in this system (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E,F.

claim: TNF-α promotes apoptosis in the HF system.
source: Compared to controls, TNF-α inhibited animals had dramatically reduced numbers of cleaved caspase-3-positive cells, indicating that TNF-α promotes apoptosis in this system (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TNF-α inhibition reduces apoptosis.

claim: TNF-α is expressed by apoptotic cells in the skin and plays a physiological role to orchestrate cohort cell death during HF regression.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that in mice TNF-α is expressed by apoptotic cells in the skin, and that it plays a physiological role to orchestrate cohort cell death during HF regression.
evidence: This is inferred from the TNF-α expression and neutralization experiments.

claim: Apoptotic cells have the capacity to produce proliferative signals, such as Wg and Dpp.
source: It is becoming clear that apoptosis is not a passive phenomenon where dying cells merely die and are silently removed from the tissues. Instead, apoptotic cells have the capacity to produce proliferative signals, such as Wg and Dpp, thus serving as a crucial driving force in wound healing, regeneration and tumor formation in a variety of different organisms (Huh et al., 2004; Perez-Garijo et al., 2004; Ryoo et al., 2004; Chera et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Pellettieri et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Apoptotic cells serve as a crucial driving force in wound healing, regeneration and tumor formation in a variety of different organisms.
source: It is becoming clear that apoptosis is not a passive phenomenon where dying cells merely die and are silently removed from the tissues. Instead, apoptotic cells have the capacity to produce proliferative signals, such as Wg and Dpp, thus serving as a crucial driving force in wound healing, regeneration and tumor formation in a variety of different organisms (Huh et al., 2004; Perez-Garijo et al., 2004; Ryoo et al., 2004; Chera et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Pellettieri et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Dying cells can generate pro-apoptotic signals that induce apoptosis in neighboring cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that signaling by apoptotic cells is not limited to the production of proliferative signals: dying cells can generate pro-apoptotic signals that induce apoptosis in neighboring cells.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The induction of apoptosis by dying cells is triggered by Eiger, which activates the JNK pathway and leads to cell death in a non-autonomous manner.
source: We show that the induction of this apoptosis is triggered by Eiger, the ortholog of TNF in Drosophila, which in turn activates the JNK pathway and leads to cell death in a non-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: TNF-α is required for coordinated cell death in the HF.
source: Significantly, TNF-α is required for coordinated cell death in the HF.
evidence: This is supported by TNF-α neutralization experiments.

claim: AiA plays an important physiological role for the coordination of cohort cell death.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that AiA plays an important physiological role for the coordination of cohort cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings in both Drosophila and mice.

claim: Induction of apoptosis in one compartment results in induction of non-autonomous apoptosis in the neighboring compartment under many different conditions.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that induction of apoptosis in one compartment results in induction of non-autonomous apoptosis in the neighboring compartment. This is true under many different conditions: both when we generate undead cells (expressing rpr/hid and p35) or upon induction of genuine apoptosis (expressing rpr/hid alone); once there is ectopic expression of mitogens that leads to excessive proliferation and growth or while blocking mitogenic production or growth of the compartment.
evidence: This summarizes the experimental findings.

claim: The regions of the wing pouch where non-autonomous cell death is observed are more prone to cell death as a response to different apoptotic stimuli.
source: In fact, the regions of the wing pouch where we observe the non-autonomous cell death are also more prone to cell death as a response to different apoptotic stimuli, such as irradiation or hid over-expression (Milan et al., 1997; Moon et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cells neighboring apoptotic cells downregulate Hippo pathway and consequently activate Diap1.
source: In fact, it has been shown that cells neighboring apoptotic cells downregulate Hippo pathway and consequently activate Diap1 (Grusche et al., 2011; Sun and Irvine, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In physiological conditions such as the coordinated cell death of HF cells in mice, signaling between apoptotic cells would be expected to occur at a much shorter range, probably affecting the immediate neighbors.
source: On the other hand, in physiological conditions such as the coordinated cell death of HF cells observed in mice, it would be expected that signaling between apoptotic cells would occur at a much shorter range, probably affecting the immediate neighbors.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The observation that TNF-α is exclusively detected in apoptotic cells and its inhibition leads to desynchronization of the HF cycle strongly suggests that AiA can be a mechanism to coordinate cell death within a tissue.
source: In any case, the observation that TNF-α is exclusively detected in apoptotic cells and the fact that its inhibition leads to desynchronization of the HF cycle strongly suggests that AiA can be a mechanism to coordinate cell death within a tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings in mice.

claim: It remains to be elucidated whether Eiger directly diffuses to the cells in the anterior compartment, or if some other mechanism is responsible for the activation of JNK in dying cells in the anterior compartment.
source: However, it remains to be elucidated whether Eiger directly diffuses to the cells in the anterior compartment, or if some other mechanism is responsible for the activation of JNK in dying cells in the anterior compartment.
evidence: This describes an open question from the study.

claim: Upon wounding, JNK activity can be propagated at a distance through a feed-forward loop.
source: Recently, it was shown that, upon wounding, JNK activity can be propagated at a distance through a feed-forward loop (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TNF-α plays a known role to promote cell death and has been previously implicated in HF progression, wound healing and regeneration.
source: TNF-α plays a known role to promote cell death and has been previously implicated in HF progression, wound healing and regeneration (Werner and Grose, 2003; Tong and Coulombe, 2006; Bohm et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It was previously not appreciated that apoptotic cells can be the source of TNF-α signals.
source: However, the cellular source of TNF-α remained unknown and it was previously not appreciated that apoptotic cells can be the source of these signals.
evidence: This describes a gap in scientific knowledge addressed by the study.

claim: AiA and at least some of the underlying mechanism have been conserved in evolution to promote coordinated cell death.
source: Our results suggest that AiA and at least some of the underlying mechanism have been conserved in evolution to promote coordinated cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings in both Drosophila and mice.

claim: Propagation of an apoptotic stimulus may be a useful mechanism to achieve the rapid and coordinated death of large cell populations.
source: On the one hand, there are situations where propagation of an apoptotic stimulus may be a useful mechanism to achieve the rapid and coordinated death of large cell populations.
evidence: This is speculation about the significance of AiA.

claim: Examples of cell death being used during development to sculpt tissues and organs include the removal of structures during metamorphosis and the separation of digits through apoptosis of the interdigital webbing in many vertebrates.
source: There are many other examples of cell death being used during development to sculpt tissues and organs, including the removal of structures during metamorphosis (tadpole tail, larval organs in insects, elimination of inappropriate sex organs in mammals, deletion of the amnio serosa during insect embryogenesis) and the separation of digits through apoptosis of the interdigital webbing in many vertebrates (Glucksmann, 1951; Jacobson et al., 1997; Fuchs and Steller, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AiA may facilitate cohort behavior and contribute to the rapid and complete elimination of large fields of cells during development.
source: In all these cases, AiA may facilitate cohort behavior and contribute to the rapid and complete elimination of large fields of cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of AiA in development.

claim: Propagation of cell death may be an efficient way to prevent infection.
source: Propagation of cell death may also be an efficient way to prevent infection.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of AiA in immunity.

claim: Cells respond to viral infection by entering apoptosis and in this way impede the replication of the virus.
source: It is known that cells respond to viral infection by entering apoptosis and in this way impede the replication of the virus (Barber, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The process of AiA would extend apoptosis to the neighboring cells, preventing also their infection and thus avoiding the spread of the virus.
source: The process of AiA would extend apoptosis to the neighboring cells, preventing also their infection and thus avoiding the spread of the virus.
evidence: This is speculation about how AiA could function in viral infection.

claim: Propagation of apoptosis may be detrimental in pathological conditions where excessive cell death underlies the etiology of the disease.
source: However, propagation of apoptosis may be detrimental in pathological conditions where excessive cell death underlies the etiology of the disease.
evidence: This is speculation about the negative consequences of AiA.

claim: This may be the case for neurodegenerative disorders, hepatic diseases, cardiac infarction, etc.
source: This may be the case for neurodegenerative disorders, hepatic diseases, cardiac infarction, etc (Thompson, 1995; Favaloro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It remains to be studied whether extensive amounts of apoptosis observed in affected tissues are a direct consequence of cell damage in an autonomous manner or if part of the cell loss could be attributed to a process of propagation through AiA.
source: In all these cases it remains to be studied whether extensive amounts of apoptosis that are observed in the affected tissues are a direct consequence of cell damage in an autonomous manner or if part of the cell loss could be attributed to a process of propagation through AiA.
evidence: This describes an open question for future research.

claim: AiA may play a role in cancer.
source: Finally, AiA may play a role in cancer.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of AiA in cancer.

claim: Radiotherapy in humans can induce biological effects in non-irradiated cells at a considerable distance, a phenomenon called radiation-induced bystander effect.
source: It is known that radiotherapy in humans can induce biological effects in non-irradiated cells at a considerable distance, a phenomenon called radiation-induced bystander effect (Hei et al., 2011; Prise and O'Sullivan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The current findings provide a possible explanation for some of the radiation-induced bystander effects.
source: Our current findings provide a possible explanation for some of these effects.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: Large-scale induction of apoptosis by AiA may contribute to successful cancer therapy.
source: Therefore, large-scale induction of apoptosis by AiA may contribute to successful cancer therapy.
evidence: This is speculation about the therapeutic implications of AiA.

claim: TNF family proteins are being used as models for drug development aimed to treat cancer.
source: TNF family proteins are being used as models for drug development aimed to treat cancer (Ashkenazi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Eiger has a known role in the elimination of pre-tumoral scrib− clones.
source: Furthermore, Eiger, the only TNF member in Drosophila, has a known role in the elimination of pre-tumoral scrib− clones (Igaki et al., 2009; Ohsawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell competition induces cell death even in aggressive scrib−RasV12 tumors.
source: In addition, cell competition induces cell death even in aggressive scrib−RasV12 tumors, raising the possibility that AiA is induced during tumor initiation, which may affect the tumor microenvironment and ultimately tumor growth (Menendez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and speculation about AiA's role.

claim: TNF can play both tumor-promoting and tumor-suppressing roles.
source: It is well known that TNF can play both tumor-promoting and tumor-suppressing roles, but AiA has not been investigated in this context (Pikarsky and Ben-Neriah, 2006; Vainer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AiA has not been investigated in the context of tumor biology prior to this study.
source: It is well known that TNF can play both tumor-promoting and tumor-suppressing roles, but AiA has not been investigated in this context (Pikarsky and Ben-Neriah, 2006; Vainer et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes a gap in scientific knowledge.
